extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, IP lawyers, and patent practitioners assessing prior‑art disclosure, novelty and inventive step
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for determining when information (including paperless/new‑media disclosures) constitutes prior art for novelty and inventive step assessments in patent law. Covers examiner practices, statutory definitions, exceptions (confidentiality, abuse), and evidentiary/timing/place considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO: official/quasi-official web-site presumed original
rubrics_metrics.description: Information on the web-site of an official or quasi-official organization which is not likely to be manipulated is presumed to be the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by examiners to minimize manipulation risk when treating internet materials as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO: examiner verification for internet content
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner is not confident of the originality, i.e. possible manipulation of the content of the web-site, he/she may contact the responsible party of the web-site to confirm the reliability of the information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contacting the responsible party is an available step before citing internet material.

rubrics_metrics.name: JPO: recordkeeping when citing internet sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the examiner decides to cite the information on the internet, he/she prints out the information and inscribes necessary information such as name of the examiner, time and date of the access and URL of the web-site onto the printed document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper prints with examiner name, access time/date, and URL are created and later stored in the JPO patent‑related database to preserve evidence of the citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese statutory categories of prior art and internet novelty criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese Patent Law classifies prior art into three categories: publicly known invention, publicly worked invention and the invention described in a distributed publication; 1999 amendment widened novelty to world basis (absolute novelty) and introduced 'the invention available through internet' as a novelty criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory categories and the explicit inclusion of internet availability shape novelty analysis in Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic novelty and inventive step formulations (Japan)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention identical to what is disclosed by the prior art lacks novelty; an invention that could have been easily made by a skilled person in the art lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard two‑part assessment used in Japanese practice: identity for novelty, obviousness-for-skilled-person for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of pending applications (Japan)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pending application that has not yet been published is prior art to the application filed later; the earlier filed applications cannot be the basis of the inventive step; co-pending applications by same applicant/inventor are resolved by double patenting or first‑to‑file principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes novelty effect of earlier pending filings from their (non‑)role in inventive step assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty defined (Netherlands working group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty: 'Subject matter that is not directly, explicitly or implicitly derivable from the state of the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes direct/explicit/implicit derivability from prior art as test for novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step defined (Netherlands working group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive Step: 'The non-obvious solution of a problem given the closest state of the art in respect of said problem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step assessment focuses on non‑obviousness in light of the closest prior art and the problem addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art disclosure defined (Netherlands working group)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art disclosure: 'Anything made available to the public by whatever means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Working group adds that recipient's individual knowledge/capacity and reproducibility of the information are relevant to whether it was made available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential effect of prior art on novelty vs inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Each piece of prior art can be detrimental for novelty; for inventive step, only prior art in the same or neighbouring technical fields (and addressing or relating to the same problem as the invention) will be taken into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A remote-field citation that addresses a completely different objective will generally not be used for inventive step rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pending applications and their effect (Netherlands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 4 (3)/(4) ROW 1995: contents of previously filed applications entered in the Dutch patent register and published European/international applications are part of the state of the art and can affect novelty; Article 6 ROW 1995: such pending applications belonging to the state of the art shall not be taken into consideration in assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes novelty impact (they can be prior art) from inventive step (they are excluded) under Dutch law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure criterion: access by a random third party
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece of prior art is generally considered to have been disclosed if a random third party could have (had) access to the prior art; it is not relevant whether the third party actually noticed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion in a library counts as public availability; submission to an individual who cannot redistribute normally does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality/abuse exception (Netherlands)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure that is a direct or indirect consequence of an evident abuse (e.g., breach of contractual confidentiality) shall be disregarded under Article 5(1) ROW 1995.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express confidentiality agreements and, under some circumstances, implied confidentiality can exclude material from being prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of disclosure: any perceptible means
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 4(2) ROW 1995 and working group: disclosure can take place by written or oral description, by use or in any other way; the disclosed information should be perceptible by the senses (hearing, vision, smell, taste etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The physical medium is irrelevant; if something can be perceived (e.g., observed by diving), it can be state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time (age) of disclosure for novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The period lapsed between disclosure and filing is not relevant for novelty (a disclosure remains prior art regardless of age); time may be relevant for inventive step since older documents are less likely to be considered relevant evidence of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess implied information at the priority date; seniority can be argued as reducing a citation's weight for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of disclosure and applicable law
rubrics_metrics.description: Once established that information has been disclosed, the place in the world is irrelevant for novelty; however, the question whether something was disclosed is to be assessed under the law applicable to the place of disclosure (conflict‑of‑law considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective day of internet publication is the local date/time at the place of disclosure; courts apply domestic conflict rules to decide which foreign law governs confidentiality/disclosure issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient ability and reproducibility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipient must have been able to realize what the invention consists of and should be able to reproduce the information in some form (skilled person standard applies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feasible reverse engineering or disassembly that would enable the skilled person counts as disclosure; if special efforts were made to prevent reverse engineering, public use may not be disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors in disclosed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in disclosed information are not harmful to novelty if it is clear from the whole context that an error has been made; if unclear to the skilled person, errors may harm novelty. Errors in summaries may affect inventive step even if the underlying disclosure did not contain the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate enabling content and whether the skilled person could correct the error without undue burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic/new media: same disclosure rules as paper
rubrics_metrics.description: No special rules yet; generally the same rules apply in an electronic or internet environment as in a paper environment — decisive factor is whether the information has been disclosed and whether a recipient is able to reproduce it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Netherlands group treats chatgroups/forums as disclosed (unless confidentiality binds members); e‑mail may be private if protected or encrypted, but unprotected e‑mail generally not treated as sealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic confidentiality factors (encryption, password, search engines, paywalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encrypted information and password‑protected content are not by nature publicly available; information that can be found by a search engine or obtained through payment is prima facie assumed to be publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recipients who can access the content can freely redistribute it, it may be treated as disclosed despite technical protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transience and archival of online disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The transience of the medium (short duration of availability) is not relevant to whether information has been made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, transience affects the ability to produce evidence of disclosure; archives and printouts are useful to preserve proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for internet disclosure (Netherlands civil procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Netherlands Code of Civil Procedure (Article 177) the burden of proof that information was disclosed on the Internet rests with the party that makes the claim; that party must submit sufficient evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claimant must present documentary/evidentiary support (prints, server logs, etc.) to establish online disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norway: broad definition of prior art and enabling requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Norwegian Patents Act: 'Everything made available to the public, either in writing, orally, by exploitation or otherwise, shall be considered as known.' To be damaging for novelty and inventive step a piece of information has to be an enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑enabling disclosures (errors not readily correctable) do not damage novelty/inventive step; Norwegian practice follows EPO Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norway: pending applications and grace exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: National pending applications not yet published at the priority date affect novelty but not inventive step. A six‑month 'grace period' may be granted for disclosures resulting from evident abuse or display at official international exhibitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to other jurisdictions: certain abusive disclosures or exhibition disclosures are disregarded within the statutory grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norway: testing/experimental-use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary testing of an embodiment is an exception from the rule that novelty is damaged if the invention has been made available to an unlimited circle of people, provided the applicant/inventor can substantiate that efforts were made to avoid public availability during testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant can show reasonable steps were taken to prevent public disclosure during tests, public use may not be considered disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norway: public embodiment and reverse engineering
rubrics_metrics.description: If an embodiment is publicly accessible and it is possible to disassemble the embodiment to reveal the invention, it is regarded as a disclosure; if special efforts were made to avoid disassembly, public use may not be disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse engineering feasibly achievable by the skilled person turns a public embodiment into prior art.
